description: In SYNERA you will find an ideal space if your interest lies in developing prototypes that help monitor the physical and mental health of astronauts during their space missions. If you love designing, analyzing, and building proposals that transcend universes, you are in the right place. We are looking for skills in software, AI, hardware, areas of mental and physical health, and above all, teamwork skills.
summary: On the ISS, a crew member who feels off can talk to a flight surgeon within minutes. On Mars a reply can take up to 44 minutes, so the crew will have to look after themselves much more. Galley is a short daily check-in for that situation. The astronaut stands at the station screen, Galley recognizes their face on the device, and the camera turns off. Then it goes through eight readings (resting heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep, mood, reaction-test lapses, food intake and exercise) and compares each one with that person's own last two weeks. A population average would mislead here, because spaceflight changes the body; core temperature rises about 1 °C on long missions. Seven rules, each backed by a published source, turn the result into one next step, anywhere from "rest and measure again" to "act now". On the ISS the report goes to Earth right away. On Mars, Galley walks the crew through what to do on board and queues the report. It works offline and uses real NASA data from DONKI and OSDR. It is decision support and does not diagnose anything.
details:
What it does

Galley brings daily health readings into one screen so a crew member can see what has changed, understand why it matters and choose a next step. It combines a short daily log, a personal baseline and a body-shaped display. The check-in is designed to take about a minute, excluding the reaction-time test. We have not yet measured completion time with astronauts.

The body display groups related readings. It does not scan the body, locate an injury or show which organ is affected. The head groups sleep, mood, reaction-test lapses and skin temperature. The chest shows resting heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂). The abdomen shows food intake as a percentage of planned calories, and the legs show exercise as a percentage of prescribed minutes. These positions help users find information quickly. They do not indicate where each measurement was taken.

The hardware design uses an ESP32, a MAX30102 fingertip sensor and a skin-temperature probe to send readings over USB once per second. We could not obtain a physical board during the hackathon, so the demonstration uses a clearly labelled, 14-day simulated dataset, while the firmware runs in Wokwi. The demo therefore shows the planned data flow without claiming that we tested the sensors on people.

Sleep, mood, reaction-test results, food intake and exercise come from the daily log. Galley does not measure blood glucose or blood pressure, and neither produces alerts in this prototype.

When a reading or combination of readings needs attention, Galley displays a suggested next step. More serious patterns also produce a draft S-B-A-R report: Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. This gives a flight surgeon a short account of what changed, the relevant history, the rule that was triggered and the proposed follow-up.

The prototype models different communication conditions for the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Immediate delivery and delayed reporting are simulated behaviours, rather than connections to an operational medical communication system.

How it works

Galley compares daily readings with the person’s recent history. Its baseline calculation uses a 14-day history and excludes the three most recent days to reduce the chance that a developing change will immediately shift the baseline.

The engine uses the median and median absolute deviation, or MAD. These describe the centre and spread of the readings while reducing the influence of unusual values. Fixed operational thresholds are also checked and take priority when crossed.

Seven rules examine individual readings and combinations:

  • R1 — Short sleep: identifies sleep below the configured target.
  • R2 — Fatigue-related pattern: combines short sleep with increased reaction-test lapses or low mood, alongside elevated resting heart rate.
  • R3 — Low food intake: identifies repeated intake below the planned amount.
  • R4 — Changes requiring review: identifies a sustained rise in resting heart rate together with higher skin temperature. This pattern is not specific to infection and does not establish a diagnosis.
  • R5 — Low exercise completion: identifies several days of exercise below the prescribed target. It does not directly measure muscle loss or physical deconditioning.
  • R6 — Space-weather attention: uses solar particle event records or proton-flux thresholds to provide environmental context.
  • R7 — Escalation: combines serious findings and prepares an S-B-A-R report.

The four action levels are self-care, notify the crew, consult the flight surgeon and urgent review. These are prototype categories. They have not been clinically validated for use during space missions.

The browser runs the TypeScript decision engine compiled to JavaScript. Automated tests check selected calculations and rule behaviours. Those tests verify software behaviour; they do not establish medical accuracy.

How NASA data contributes

Galley separates simulated daily health readings from real NASA datasets.

The space-weather card replays historical solar particle events from the May 2024 storm using NASA DONKI records. Where proton flux is used, the threshold refers to protons with energies of at least 10 MeV. The display identifies the event date and source so users can distinguish a historical replay from a current alert.

A solar event provides environmental context. It does not show how much radiation a particular astronaut received or whether that person experienced a health effect.

A separate card presents blood glucose and white blood cell measurements from four Inspiration4 crew members, available through NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. Their preflight measurements illustrate how personal baselines can differ, even among people taking part in the same mission.

In our review, average preflight glucose values ranged from approximately 71 to 80 mg/dL. These differences helped us explain the purpose of personal baselines. They do not validate Galley’s rules for sleep, fatigue or cardiovascular monitoring.

Three participants also had low glucose values recorded at R+45, meaning 45 days after return. Their cause was not established in our review, so we retain those measurements with a note asking users to interpret them cautiously.

Each daily indicator also includes a “What does this mean?” panel. It explains the measurement, its connection to spaceflight health risks, the personal comparison and the suggested next step, with links to relevant NASA Human Research Program resources.

Designed for the crew’s day

Crew schedules leave little room for long forms. Galley keeps the main screen focused on readings that need attention, while charts and explanations remain available for closer review.

The interface supports English and Spanish. It uses Atkinson Hyperlegible, and every status includes a word and an icon alongside its colour. Users should be able to understand a status without relying on colour alone.

The design includes a dim, warm pre-sleep theme inspired by the ISS approach to lighting before rest. We describe it as a reduced-blue colour palette rather than claiming that a screen emits no blue light.

Face recognition is designed to run locally, with the camera active only during identification. The privacy goal is to keep camera images on the device and separate identification from any health report that may later be shared. Offline operation is also a design priority, using locally stored application files, reference data, face models and voice clips. Complete offline coverage still requires testing across browsers and devices.

What makes the approach different

Galley combines personal trends, clear explanations and mission context in one workflow. A crew member can inspect the baseline, see which rule was triggered and understand the reason for a suggested action.

Distance from Earth changes how that information must be used. Communication with Mars can involve delays of up to about 22 minutes each way, before allowing for the time needed to review a report and prepare a response. Galley therefore models local guidance alongside delayed reporting. It does not assume that a flight surgeon can answer immediately.

The visual design draws from labelled panels and equipment tags used inside the ISS. Our aim was to make readings easy to find and compare, especially when someone is tired. Testing with intended users is needed to find out whether that layout works as well for them as it did for our team.

Why we think it helps

Galley explores a practical question: how can a person understand a change in their health when expert support is far away or temporarily unavailable?

Our answer is to show the change clearly, explain the evidence behind the alert and prepare a concise report for further review. The rules remain visible, and simulated data is identified throughout the demonstration.

We are from Bolivia, where distance and unreliable connections can also make specialist care difficult to reach. This motivated us to consider future uses in remote clinics, field teams and polar stations. Any adaptation would need local evaluation. High-altitude communities, for example, require careful consideration of oxygen saturation, and a personal baseline alone cannot establish a safe threshold.

Galley is a hackathon decision-support prototype, not a clinically validated medical device. The next steps are to test physical sensors, verify offline behaviour, evaluate usability and review the alert rules with qualified health professionals before considering operational use.
